newsitem.title: UK: British markets spooked by election jitters.
newsitem.headline: British markets spooked by election jitters.

text.p: A bout of pre-election nerves grabbed hold of British financial markets on Monday as Prime Minister John Major set the poll date for May 1.

The announcement of the election date had been long awaited but last minute jitters, mainly by international investors, pushed sterling almost three pfennigs lower against the mark and weighed on stocks and bonds, dealers said.
"Political worries are no good for markets," said one senior equities trader. "When people actually see it in the headlines they take notice of it."

The pound was the main victim. It came under selling pressure ahead of the announcement, dropping to its lowest level against the mark in six weeks as investors liquidated long sterling positions, with one U.S. hedge fund noted a major seller.

At 1415 GMT, sterling traded at 2.6855 marks, up a touch from session lows at 2.6638, but down from 2.7125 in late European trading on Friday. Against the generally softer dollar, it was also weaker at $1.5932 from $1.6012 late on Friday.

The FTSE 100 index of leading shares was at 4375.8, down 47.8 points, or over one percent, from the previous close. U.K. gilts, (government bonds) also weakened slightly, with the June futures contract down 5/32 at 110-17 at 1330 GMT.
Dealers pointed to profit-taking pressures after sterling's sizzling rally and the FTSE's recent rise to record highs.
Nerves about another sell-off on Wall Street also knocked confidence, while stock market heavy-weights going ex dividend also pushed the FTSE lower.

But market attention in the next few weeks is likely to focus on the progress of the lengthy election campaign and opinion polls on the standing of the two main parties. The opinion polls clearly favour a victory by the opposition Labour Party.
Even though investors have taken a sanguine view of a Labour win, analysts pointed to sterling's rocky history ahead of polls.
The last six general elections were preceded by a tendency of the pound to weaken, said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

On average, it fell by 2.6 percent against the mark although the pre-election decline has moderated a bit since the 1970s. In 1983 and October 1974, last minute nerves dragged the pound to its low just a day before votes were cast.

In the past, the prospect of a Labour victory would have sent the markets shuddering because of its reputation as a high-spending, punitive-taxation party. But "Old Labour" has been thoroughly reformed.
Labour leader Tony Blair on Monday reiterated the party had changed for good and there would be no return to the days of a much more left-wing Labour Party.
"If anything, (a Labour victory) could be a mild positive ...," said Roger Francis, senior analyst at IBJ International in London.
"Labour looks to be willing to keep tight fiscal and monetary policy in the near-term, and maybe more accommodative to (European) monetary union," he said.
Joe Rooney, strategist at Lehman Brothers, said the election date announcement will hardly change perceptions towards the British equity market.

"Markets are supposed to be rational discounters and there had been plenty of time to digest this...The (UK stock) market looks good value relative to European and other global markets and once the election is out of the way I think we will be able to focus back on the fundamentals," said Rooney.

At the last general election, in April 1992, opinion polls predicted either a narrow Labour victory or a hung parliament. Once it became clear, Major's Conservative government had retained power, British financial markets rallied.
The worst possible outcome for Britain's financial markets would be no overall majority for either of the two main political parties, analysts said.
An inconclusive election result would mean both major parties would concentrate on trying to win over voters rather than making potentially unpopular decisions on interest rates or taxes.

"If you get a hung parliament there will be worries that another election is imminent and that both monetary and fiscal policy would be looser than they ought to be," said David Walton, UK economist at Goldman Sachs. -- London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
